title: Rethinking Multimodal Learning from the Perspective of Mitigating Classific

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states the method achieves 'competitive performance, outperforming several recent baselines by a modest margin' and notes 'some results exhibit overlapping confidence intervals with prior work, indicating the improvements may not be universally significant.' However, the Introduction claims 'Experiments reveal that our approach can outperform SOTA baselines to achieve the best performance by a large margin' and the Conclusion repeats 'our proposed method can achieve state-of-the-art performance compared with various baselines by a large margin.' These are directly contradictory characterizations of the same results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 (Eq. 2 to Eq. 6) and Section 4.4 Ablation Study
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main text defines Equation (2) (residual labels) and then jumps directly to Equation (6) (overall loss), skipping Equations (3), (4), and (5), which are never shown or defined. Yet Section 4.4 explicitly references 'the key components of our objectives in Equation (2), (3), and (4)' (denoted ε, ε_o, ε_p) and the text itself notes 'summing classification loss for current classifier, all classifiers, and previous classifiers in Equation (5) may double-count errors.' These equations are referenced and analyzed but never actually presented, making the method's core loss formulation unverifiable and internally inconsistent.

The adaptive classifier assignment rule uses the same threshold τ for both branches: 'if s_t^a − σ s_t^v > τ then Add classifier for video' and 'else if s_t^a − σ s_t^v < τ then Add classifier for audio.' Since the second condition is only reached when the first is false (i.e., when the difference ≤ τ), the audio branch will trigger whenever the difference is not greater than τ, including values arbitrarily close to τ but not negative. This leaves no actual 'dead zone' for fault tolerance as claimed, and the lower bound should logically be '< −τ' for a symmetric tolerance region around 0.

The paper claims 'we utilize y_i to mask non-ground-truth labels to ensure the non-negativity of residual labels,' but masking only zeroes out non-ground-truth entries; it does not prevent the ground-truth entry itself from going negative. Since λ ∈ [0,1] and the sum of probabilities from multiple prior classifiers (each up to 1) can exceed 1/λ, the residual value y_i − λΣp_ij can become negative for the true class, contradicting the stated guarantee.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix Table II vs. Table III
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table II reports accuracy for #CLS=10 (the final classifier count used by 'Ours') as 0.8515 (ζ=0), 0.8280 (ζ=20), and 0.8145 (ζ=50). Table III, reporting the same method ('Ours') under the same noise conditions, lists 0.8515 (ζ=0), 0.8333 (ζ=20), and 0.8253 (ζ=50). The ζ=20 and ζ=50 values differ between the two tables for what should be the identical final model/result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix C.2 vs. main text citations for G-Blend
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Throughout the main text (Abstract, Introduction, Figure 1 caption, Table 1), G-Blend is cited as reference [40] (Wang, Tran, Feiszli). However, Appendix C.2 cites it as '[10]', and reference [10] in the bibliography is listed as 'W. et al. What Makes Training Multi-Modal Classification Networks Hard? CoRR... 2020' — an incomplete/duplicate entry for the same paper already properly cited as [40], indicating a fabricated or duplicated citation.

The text states 'Similarly, MLA [50] applies alternating adaptation strategies between modalities to encourage balanced joint training. These approaches leverage boosting concepts as part of a broader multi-modal interaction framework.' However, MLA is described in the same paragraph (and elsewhere) as an alternating training algorithm, not a boosting-based method; attributing 'boosting concepts' to MLA misrepresents its actual mechanism (only ReconBoost explicitly uses boosting).

The text admits: 'While the proposed method uses cross-validated hyperparameters and tailored learning rate schedules, the baselines were run using authors' default configurations or publicly available checkpoints without further tuning. This may imbalance the comparison favoring the proposed method due to unequal training optimizations.' This represents an acknowledged methodological flaw that undermines the validity of the claimed performance gains reported in Table 1.

The proof introduces an additional unstated assumption mid-derivation: 'Suppose that two modalities achieve the same optimal value, i.e., L^a(Φ*) = L^v(Φ*).' This condition is not part of any of the five listed Assumptions (1–5), yet it is required to derive Eq. (29)–(34) and ultimately Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, constituting an unjustified addition to the formal proof.

The abstract and Section 3.4 claim the theoretical analysis 'ensur[es] the effectiveness of the proposed boosting scheme,' yet the same section immediately concedes: 'these conditions do not strictly hold for practical deep learning models... Empirical observations in Section 4 suggest a trend toward convergence but do not conclusively verify the convergence rate or conditions theoretically claimed.' This directly contradicts the claim that the theory 'ensures' effectiveness.
